content: 1. Cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, blood triglycerides, and insulin are key biomarkers often analyzed in medical and health-related research. 2. A systematic review by Errisuriz VL, Golaszewski NM, Born K, and Bartholomew JB in 2018 examined physical education (PE)-based interventions aimed at improving physical activity (PA), fitness, and body composition in elementary school children. The review also provided recommendations for future research directions. 3. The review included experimental and quasi-experimental studies conducted in elementary schools. A total of 4,964 studies were initially identified, but only 12 met the eligibility criteria after abstract and full-text screening. 4. The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using criteria established by Downs and Black (1998). PE interventions consistently increased moderate-to-vigorous PA during PE classes but had less consistent effects on leisure-time PA, body mass index (BMI), or skinfold thickness. 5. Half of the studies assessing fitness outcomes showed no significant impact, except for those specifically designed to influence fitness. Few studies evaluated psychosocial determinants of PA, and none demonstrated significant impacts beyond knowledge improvement. 6. The review highlighted the need for future research to use more objective and accurate measurements of PA and adiposity, incorporate psychological constructs, expand theoretical frameworks, and include robust process evaluations. 7. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Fang K and Mu M in 2019 estimated the relationship between screen time and childhood overweight/obesity. The study found a positive association between increased screen time and higher risk of overweight/obesity in children under 18 years. 8. Data from 16 studies published up to May 2019 were included. The analysis revealed that prolonged screen time is a risk factor for childhood overweight/obesity due to reduced physical activity and increased energy intake. 9. A systematic review by Koedijk JB and Rijswijk et al. in 2017 examined the association between sedentary behavior (SB) and bone health in children, adolescents, and young adults. The review included 17 observational studies and found that objectively measured SB was negatively associated with lower extremity bone outcomes, such as femoral neck bone mineral density. 10. However, there was insufficient evidence for an association between SB and lumbar spine bone outcomes. High-quality studies using DXA showed no association between SB and total body bone outcomes. 11. A systematic review by Krahenbühl T and Guimarães RF in 2018 explored the influence of physical activity and sports on bone geometry in children and adolescents. The review included 21 studies and found that activities like gymnastics and soccer positively influenced bone geometry and bone mineral density. 12. Sports involving weight-bearing and higher intensity were more beneficial for bone geometry compared to non-weight-bearing activities like swimming. 13. A systematic review by Lee, Pope, and Gao in 2018 examined the impact of youth sports participation on daily physical activity and pediatric obesity in children aged 6 to 19. The review included 27 studies and found that greater engagement in organized youth sports was associated with higher levels of physical activity. 14. Evidence for the association between youth sports participation and obesity-related outcomes was mixed and inconsistent. Most studies relied on self-reported measures of physical activity, limiting the reliability of findings. 15. A meta-analysis by Marker C, Gnambs T, and Appel M in 2019 investigated the relationship between sedentary video gaming and body mass. The analysis included 20 studies and found a small and inconsistent association between video gaming and body mass, primarily observed in adults. 16. The study also tested the displacement effect of physical activity by video gaming time and found little evidence to support this hypothesis. 17. A systematic review by Marques A, Santos DA, Hillman CH, and Sardinha LB examined the relationship between academic achievement, cardiorespiratory fitness, and physical activity in children and adolescents aged 6 to 18. The review synthesized evidence from studies published between 2000 and 2016.
